analysis.one_liner: Requires gun makers to submit ballistics fingerprints of every new firearm to a federal crime database.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms to build a national database of ballistics information — the marks a gun leaves on bullets and shell casings, sometimes called ballistic fingerprints. Firearm manufacturers would have had to file this information for every new gun within 30 days of making it, and any law enforcement agency could request the data to help trace guns used in crimes. Violations could bring fines, up to 20 years in prison, or loss of the manufacturer's federal license.
analysis.who_benefits: Police and investigators solving shootings: with a ballistics database, a shell casing found at a crime scene could be matched to the gun that fired it, and from there to the dealer and buyer who bought that gun. Communities burdened by gun violence would gain a new tracing tool.

how_it_helps.text: The ATF must create a National Firearms Ballistics Database of ballistic characteristics of firearms, and must make that information available on request to any law enforcement agency or officer.
Firearm manufacturers must provide the prescribed ballistics information to the database within 30 days after manufacturing each firearm, so new guns are traceable by their ballistics from the start.

Violations carry real teeth: knowingly failing to file is punishable by fine, up to 20 years' imprisonment, or both, and a manufacturer that violates the requirement can have its federal license revoked.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers, who would bear the cost of testing every new gun and filing its ballistics data with the federal government, and who would face fines, prison exposure, and license revocation for failing to comply.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new testing and record-keeping burden on every firearm manufacturer, with criminal penalties of up to 20 years for noncompliance — a serious enforcement regime for a paperwork mandate.

The database would only cover guns made after enactment, so it would take years to accumulate enough coverage to be broadly useful, and the bill contains no funding or technology provisions for building or maintaining the database.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a national tool for matching crime-scene shell casings to specific guns — is real but slow-acting, since only newly made guns would be in the system. The cost falls narrowly on manufacturers as compliance work and penalty exposure, not on gun owners directly. Honest opponents would note the bill was thin on implementation details (funding, accuracy standards, retention of data), but its core mechanism mirrors ballistics-tracing programs later used by law enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2000, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then sent to its Crime subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Gun Ballistics Safety Act of 2000 on September 12, 2000, joined by Rep. McCarthy of New York.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and on September 21 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
The bill had only two cosponsors, both Democrats, giving it no visible path to floor consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers are better off: no federal ballistics-filing requirement, no related fines or license-revocation exposure, and no database for police to query. Police and communities affected by gun shootings did not get the tracing tool.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require manufacturers to file ballistics data with the ATF.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy
for.role: Original cosponsor, U.S. House of Representatives (NY)

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearms law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have required every manufacturer to test and file ballistics data for each new gun within 30 days, backed by fines, up to 20 years in prison, and license revocation for violations. Killing the bill spared manufacturers those compliance costs and penalties; the cost to the public is that new guns leave no ballistics record police can query when tracing crime guns.

The bill would have given any law enforcement agency or officer on-request access to a national ballistics database for crime solving. The bill's death means police keep doing ballistics matching gun by gun, without a national reference system.
